independent_deductions: For a<b with f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), MVT asserts existence of at least one c strictly between a,b such that fprime(c)=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). It does not require derivatives at endpoints or a continuous derivative, give uniqueness, or permit choosing an arbitrary c. If x<a in the renamed-endpoint form, c lies between x and a; for x=a there is no strictly interior point, though the zero-displacement identity itself is trivial.

To justify the shifted-parallel-line proof, let m=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a) and g(t)=f(t)-f(a)-m(t-a). Then g is continuous on the compact interval, differentiable inside, and g(a)=g(b)=0. If g is identically zero every interior c works. Otherwise g has a positive maximum or negative minimum at an interior point; Fermat gives gprime(c)=0 and hence fprime(c)=m. Existence of the extremum and its interior location are required steps, not consequences of an informal drawing alone. Figure 1 shows the intended parallel tangent and secant.

For absolute value with a<0<b, the secant slope (a+b)/(b-a) is strictly between -1 and 1; existing derivatives away from zero are only -1 and 1. No interior derivative equals this slope and the cusp lacks a derivative. Figure 2 thus illustrates failure of the differentiability hypothesis. The source assertion that the first contact is at zero no matter the slope is limited to its straddling-zero secant setting: slopes ±1 can coincide with a whole branch, and more extreme slopes do not have that property.

MVT makes f(x)=f(a)+fprime(c)(x-a) exact for an unspecified suitable c. Linearization instead uses the known derivative at a and is approximate; differentiability gives f(a+h)=f(a)+fprime(a)h+o(|h|). Figure 3 shows a convex example with positive signed error; no universal error sign or quantitative bound follows from that drawing. One cannot replace fprime(c) by fprime(a) as an exact equality.

On a common interval, for any a<b the equality f(b)-f(a)=fprime(c)(b-a) proves strict increasing behaviour from fprime>0, strict decreasing behaviour from fprime<0, and constancy from fprime=0. Source p4 incorrectly defines decreasing using the same inequality as increasing: the correct relation is f(a)>f(b). Across disconnected domains none of these global comparisons follows solely from the derivative: -1/x has positive derivative but its values at -1 and 1 are 1 and -1; a function equal to 0 for negative x and 1 for positive x has zero derivative throughout its domain but is not globally constant.

The stipulated trip has average scalar rate 1000/3 miles per hour. To identify the derivative with speed, f should be accumulated path distance or a monotone coordinate along the stated route, with continuity and differentiability as required. Literal distance from Boston along an arbitrary curved trajectory gives a radial rate instead. The source stipulates the 1000-mile model; it is not a current factual route-length claim.

For Rn(x)=exp(x)-sum(k=0..n)x^k/k!, Rn(0)=0 and Rnprime=R(n-1) for n>=1. Starting with R0prime=exp(x)>0, induction and the derivative-sign result establish Rn(x)>0 for x>0. This justifies the displayed positive-x finite truncation inequalities. At zero each comparison with a Taylor polynomial is equality; exp(x)>1+x is strict also for negative x, but the quadratic lower bound is not: exp(-1)<1/2. Source p5 switches f1 to undefined f in one intermediate proof comparison; it should remain f1.

The infinite-series equality needs a separate convergence argument and does not follow merely because every finite truncation is below exp(x) for positive x. For fixed real x, Taylor remainder magnitude is at most exp(|x|)|x|^(n+1)/(n+1)!, which tends to zero (successive magnitude ratio |x|/(n+2) eventually <=1/2). This proves the announced limit when the theorem and remainder are supplied; the source explicitly postpones the series topic.
All checks are direct mathematics applied to the complete provided packet. No external current factual lookup was required.
